prompt.context: Our client is a major British electricity utility. Currently, rates and returns are regulated, but a new proposal would change the system to a more market-based pool system. The mechanics (simplified for case use) are as follows: Rather than each utility producing electricity for the use of its customers only (with excess or shortage made up for in short-term contracts with other utilities or independent power producers), all utilities and power producers will bid into a pool for power supply. Bidding can be assumed to occur continuously — if a supplier decides to produce an amount of electricity (kilowatt-hours) at a certain time, he bids that amount into the pool. Bids will be arranged according to price: the producer who bids the lowest price will have his power used first, then the next highest price, etc. Demand will determine how much power gets taken from the pool at any time. The last unit of power purchased will be bought at the price it was bid into the pool at, and all power sold at that time will be sold at that same price — this is the market-clearing price.
prompt.question: How would you evaluate this situation? At what price will/should people bid into the pool? What non-competitive aspects might you expect from this system?

exhibits.title: Supply and Demand Graph for the Electricity Pool
exhibits.shows: A supply/demand graph illustrating the pool bidding mechanism, showing a step-function supply curve (chunks of power bid at different quantities and prices), an inelastic demand curve, a market-clearing price P*, and the resulting producer surplus for low-cost bidders
exhibits.data: Market-clearing price P*; step-function supply curve segments representing individual bids; vertical (inelastic) demand curve; shaded producer surplus area for low-cost producers; the last seller in the pool sells only part of his bid; the next seller sells nothing

framework: Draw a supply/demand graph: step-function supply curve (bids arranged by price) intersecting an inelastic demand curve
Identify the market-clearing price P* — the price of the last unit sold sets the price for all units
Analyze bidding strategy: producers bid at their marginal cost of production
Evaluate sustainability: assess whether equilibrium holds in the short run vs. long run
Identify strategic advantages: owning both high-cost and low-cost resources; understanding demand patterns
Assess non-competitive/collusion risks: price-fixing, signaling, gamesmanship
Consider structural characteristics of electricity generation: non-dispatchable low-cost resources (hydro, nuclear) and their implications
Draw analogies to deregulated industries: airlines (bid SRMC, lose money long-term) vs. telecom (high profits post-deregulation)

questions.prompt: How does the pool market clear, and what does the supply/demand graph look like?
questions.guidance: Candidate should draw a supply curve as a step function (each bid is a chunk of power at a given price) and a near-vertical (inelastic) demand curve. The market clears at P* — the price of the marginal (last) unit sold. The last producer in the pool sells only part of his bid; the next producer sells nothing. Low-cost producers who bid in early earn substantial producer surplus.

questions.prompt: At what price should producers bid into the pool?
questions.guidance: Producers should bid at their short-run marginal cost (SRMC). If you are the last seller, you at least break even on a short-run basis. If your cost is lower than the market-clearing price, you earn profit. Bidding above SRMC risks not being selected; bidding below SRMC results in a loss on those units.

questions.prompt: Is this bidding equilibrium sustainable in the long run?
questions.guidance: The equilibrium is not sustainable in the long run unless demand fluctuates enough to bring high-cost producers into the pool frequently. High-cost producers need to earn more than their long-run marginal cost (LRMC) on average, or they will shut down. Sustained low demand could eliminate high-cost capacity, reducing supply diversity.

questions.prompt: What strategic advantages does this system create, and what collusion risks arise?
questions.guidance: The system places a premium on owning both high-cost and low-cost resources. A firm that anticipates a demand surge can bid its high-cost resource to set the market-clearing price while simultaneously bidding its low-cost resources to capture the spread as profit. This creates obvious collusion and price-fixing concerns. The degree to which the market disciplines such behavior depends on: number and size of competitors, trade associations, degree of communication, and signaling mechanisms.

questions.prompt: What are the implications of non-dispatchable low-cost resources (e.g., hydro, nuclear)?
questions.guidance: The lowest-cost resources (hydro, nuclear) are often non-dispatchable — they must run continuously if run at all. All bidders know this, so they assume these producers bid into the pool at or near zero. During periods of slack demand, if all producers have such resources, there may be no buyers at any price and the pool will clear near zero. This makes understanding and potentially modifying demand patterns critical.

brainstorming.prompt: What non-competitive aspects and broader industry dynamics might you expect from this pool system?

categories.name: Price Collusion and Market Power
ideas: High-cost producer sets the market-clearing price, creating incentive for price-fixing
Firms with knowledge of competitors' costs can signal or coordinate bids
Few large competitors increase collusion likelihood

categories.name: Strategic Resource Ownership
ideas: Premium on owning both high-cost (price-setting) and low-cost (profit-capturing) resources
Vertical integration advantages for firms that understand demand patterns
Ability to time bids to coincide with anticipated demand peaks

categories.name: Demand Management
ideas: Understanding demand patterns is critical to profitable bidding
Modifying demand (e.g., interruptible contracts, demand response) can protect margins
Inelastic short-run demand gives suppliers pricing power

categories.name: Long-Run Sustainability
ideas: If high-cost producers cannot recover LRMC, capacity will exit the market
Reduced capacity diversity increases system reliability risk
Regulators may need to intervene to ensure adequate capacity investment

categories.name: Non-Dispatchable Resource Dynamics
ideas: Hydro and nuclear must run continuously, forcing near-zero bids during low demand
Pool price can collapse to near zero during slack periods
Creates volatility and makes long-term investment decisions difficult

categories.name: Industry Analogies
ideas: Airline deregulation: firms bid SRMC, consumers benefit short-term, but industry loses money on huge fixed costs long-term
Telecom deregulation: produced high profits — outcome depends on market structure
Deregulated market outcomes are highly sensitive to number of players and competitive dynamics

recommendation: The client should prepare to bid at short-run marginal cost (SRMC) for each generating unit to maximize pool participation
The client should prioritize acquiring or retaining a portfolio of both low-cost baseload (profit-capturing) and high-cost peaking (price-setting) resources
The client must invest in demand forecasting capabilities to time bids optimally and capture producer surplus
The client should engage proactively with regulators on market design, particularly around collusion risk and non-dispatchable resource treatment
risks: Pool price volatility and potential collapse to near-zero during slack demand periods
Long-run capacity adequacy risk if high-cost producers exit the market
Regulatory intervention risk if collusion or price manipulation is perceived
Non-dispatchable resource owners may undercut pool prices, squeezing margins
next_steps: Model historical and projected demand patterns to assess bidding strategy under various scenarios
Benchmark portfolio against competitors to identify cost position and strategic gaps
Engage legal and regulatory counsel on antitrust implications of pool bidding strategies
Evaluate demand-side management partnerships to reduce exposure to slack-demand price collapses
